The turbine blade is a hollow blade made of single-crystal PWA 1480 superalloy.
The blade span is along the [001] crystallographic direction (primary orientation) with a maximum allowable angular deviation of 10 degrees.
The thermal gradient through the blade thickness is much higher (875 °C/cm) than the gradient along the span.
The finite element model consisted of 959 eight-node isoparametric brick elements and 1575 nodes.

The thermal boundary conditions incorporated conduction through the thickness, convection between the blade surface and the flow of hot-cold gases, and convection along the surface of the hollow core section.
The mechanical loads included gas pressures and centrifugal forces produced by the blade rotational speed of 37,000 rpm.
The highest stresses were observed at the 45 degree secondary orientation.
The influence of the primary orientation angle (0-10 degrees) was much lower than the influence of the secondary orientation.
Stress concentrations were observed at the airfoil base near the leading edge, the shank leading and trailing edges below the platform, and the shank base center section.
Hardware evidence showed that these critical locations experienced cracking and other durability problems.
The effect of crystal orientation on the stresses under predominantly mechanical loading was minimal.
The current analysis was limited to an elastic stress analysis, restricting the applicability to inelastic conditions.
This study aimed to further investigate the crystal orientation effects on the elastic response of the SSME turbine blade under actual operating conditions.
The main difference from previous investigations was the use of actual operating conditions rather than simulated conditions.
The study confirmed the previous findings that the influence of secondary orientation is more significant than the primary orientation.
